title: Why Bogs Preserve Bodies for Thousands of Years
summary:
In August 1984, peat cutters near Wilmslow, south of Manchester, England, found a body in a peat bog. Known as the Lindow Man, it had lain there for nearly 2,000 years, yet was still recognizably human. He is one of at least 2,000 bog bodies recovered from Europe's peatlands, dating from the Mesolithic period, which ended in Europe between 8,500 and 5,500 years ago, through to World War II.

A peat bog is an acidic, nutrient-poor wetland made of peat, soft, spongy ground consisting of partly decayed plant material building up over hundreds or thousands of years. Peat is organic matter that builds up faster than it decays, but it mostly consists of sphagnum moss, a moisture-loving moss that stores a lot of water.

That waterlogged moss leaves little air in the bog, the first key to preservation. Bogs get almost all their water from rain and snow, so they are low in minerals and nutrients, and the water barely moves. Thick layers of decomposed material choke off the air below. Without oxygen, the environment becomes highly acidic, and bacteria and fungi that would normally break down dead material cannot thrive.

Instead, the high acidity essentially pickles a body, like a brine stopping harmful bacteria from growing. Author Anna North describes preserved bodies as living time capsules. Sphagnum moss also releases a carbohydrate called sphagnan, which binds to proteins in skin and tissue, turning skin leathery and dark-brown, like tea, while protecting it against decay. Skin, hair, nails, and internal organs can therefore remain remarkably intact for thousands of years.

Bones fare differently: acid leaches calcium from them, so they can soften, warp, or dissolve completely. Raised bogs, deep dome-shaped peatlands wetter and higher than surrounding land, preserve bodies best because they are highly acidic and entirely without oxygen.
why_it_matters: Because bogs can preserve bodies for thousands of years, they give scientists a rare window into people and times that would otherwise be lost.

background_read: A peat bog is a wetland where dead plant material builds up faster than it breaks down, forming soft, spongy ground.
Because the ground is waterlogged and still, little air reaches below the surface, and the water becomes highly acidic.
Without oxygen, the bacteria and fungi that normally break down dead material cannot thrive, so soft tissue can survive far longer than usual.
That is why bogs can preserve skin, hair, and organs, even though their acid weakens bones by removing calcium.
